summary:
NW Rota-1 is an active submarine volcano in the Mariana Islands, northwest of Rota. It matters because it was the first volcano where explosive underwater eruptions were directly observed, in 2004.

The steep seamount’s summit lies 517 metres below sea level. Eruptions observed from 2004 to 2010 produced lava, ash and other debris. The unstable deposits triggered underwater landslides, including a major collapse in August 2009 that stripped part of the southern flank. These events generated ash-rich underwater plumes.

Hydrothermal vents release sulfur, gases and an estimated 400,000 tonnes of carbon dioxide per year. The vents support microbial mats and animal communities, though frequent eruptions limit their diversity. Activity continued to vary through 2010; a 2014 remotely operated vehicle dive found no eruption.
